## Introduction

Multiple imputation with `mice()` creates `m` imputed data sets by
running `m` chains of the Gibbs sampler. Chain `i` only uses its own
imputations from the previous iteration, so the chains are independent
and can run at the same time on different cores or machines.

`mice()` can do this itself with the argument `future = TRUE`. This
builds the parallel run into `mice()`, instead of the wrapper functions
`parlmice()` (deprecated) and `futuremice()` [@volker-2022-1]. The chains
run as futures of the `future` framework [@bengtsson-2021-1], so the same
code runs on a laptop, a workstation or a cluster. You choose where the
chains run by setting a `future` plan; `mice()` itself never changes it.

This vignette shows how to use `future = TRUE`, what stays the same,
and what to watch out for. The companion vignette
[Parallel imputation: benchmarks](parallel-benchmark.html) shows when
running in parallel pays off, and how `mice(future = TRUE)` compares
to `futuremice()`.

Parallel imputation needs the `future` and `future.apply` packages:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages(c("future", "future.apply"))
```

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(mice)
library(future)
```

## Basic use

Set a plan with workers, and add `future = TRUE` to the call:

```{r}
plan(multisession, workers = 2)
imp <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, seed = 123, future = TRUE)
imp
```

`mice()` first sets up the imputation model and the starting
imputations, exactly as for `future = FALSE`. It then sends chain
`i`, with all its `maxit` iterations, to a worker, and combines the
results into one `mids` object. With `print = TRUE` (the default),
`mice()` reports the plan, the number of workers that ran the chains,
and the total time, rather than the iteration history. The same
information is stored in the result:

```{r}
imp$future[c("plan", "workers")]
```

`mice()` never uses more workers than there are chains, so `m = 5`
keeps at most five workers busy. The workers come on top of your own R
session, the main process. The main process sets up the imputation
model and the starting imputations, sends the chains to the workers,
and collects and combines the results. While the chains run, it mostly
waits. A common choice is therefore to leave one core free for it,
e.g. `plan(multisession, workers = parallelly::availableCores(omit = 1))`.

## The plan is yours

`mice()` uses the current plan as is. It does not start workers itself,
and it does not change or close the plan. This has three consequences.

* **Workers are reused.** Starting a worker takes time, mainly because
  each worker has to load `mice` and its dependencies. On a recent
  laptop this costs about a second, which is more than the whole
  imputation of a small data set. The first call with `future = TRUE`
  loads `mice` on the workers, and later calls reuse them:

  ```{r}
  imp1 <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, seed = 1, future = TRUE, print = FALSE)
  imp2 <- mice(nhanes2, m = 5, seed = 1, future = TRUE, print = FALSE)
  ```

* **`sequential` is respected.** Under the default plan, `sequential`,
  `future = TRUE` runs the chains one after the other in your own
  session. The result is the same as on parallel workers, which is
  useful for debugging. The printed summary then reports `on 1 worker`,
  a reminder that no plan with workers was set.

* **You choose the backend.** Any `future` backend works, also those
  that `mice` does not know about. Some examples:

  ```{r, eval = FALSE}
  # forked processes, Linux and macOS outside RStudio only
  plan(multicore, workers = 8)

  # background R sessions based on mirai, with the future.mirai package
  plan(future.mirai::mirai_multisession, workers = 8)

  # R sessions on other machines
  plan(cluster, workers = c("node1", "node2", "node3"))

  # jobs on an HPC scheduler, with the future.batchtools package
  plan(future.batchtools::batchtools_slurm)
  ```

See `vignette("future-1-overview", package = "future")` for all
options. With `future = FALSE` (the default), `mice()` ignores the plan
and uses the classic sequential sampler, which performs iteration 1 for
all chains, then iteration 2 for all chains, and so on. With
`print = TRUE` (the default), it prints the iteration history while it
runs.

## Reproducibility

Each chain gets its own random number stream, derived from `seed`
(`future.seed = TRUE` in `future.apply`). As a result, the imputations
are reproducible with `future = TRUE`, and they do not depend on the
plan or the number of workers:

```{r}
imp2 <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, seed = 123, future = TRUE, print = FALSE)
plan(sequential)
imp1 <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, seed = 123, future = TRUE, print = FALSE)
plan(multisession, workers = 2)
identical(complete(imp1, "long"), complete(imp2, "long"))
```

The imputations do differ from those of `future = FALSE` with the
same seed. The classic sampler takes the random numbers for all
chains from one and the same stream, in the order in which it visits
them: iteration 1 of chain 1, iteration 1 of chain 2, and so on. With
`future = TRUE`, each chain draws from its own stream:

```{r}
imps <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, seed = 123, print = FALSE)
identical(complete(imps, "long"), complete(imp2, "long"))
```

Both are valid multiple imputations. If you need to reproduce an
earlier analysis, use the same setting of `future` as before.

## The result is an ordinary `mids` object

The object returned by `mice(future = TRUE)` has the same structure
as that of the sequential sampler. All functions that work on a `mids`
object work as before. Convergence plots use `chainMean` and
`chainVar`, which hold one trace per chain. We remove `bmi` from the
`boys` data, because it is a deterministic function of `hgt` and `wgt`,
which makes the chains mix slowly:

```{r}
boys2 <- boys[, names(boys) != "bmi"]
imp <- mice(boys2, m = 5, maxit = 10, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
            print = FALSE)
plot(imp, c("hgt", "wgt", "hc"))
```

The events that the chains log, such as removed predictors, are
collected in `loggedEvents` in the order of the sequential sampler.
The usual analysis and pooling steps are unchanged:

```{r}
fit <- with(imp, lm(wgt ~ age + hgt))
summary(pool(fit))
```

## Adding iterations

`mice.mids()` adds iterations to an existing `mids` object. An object
created with `future = TRUE` continues as futures, and the result is
the same as that of a single call with all iterations:

```{r}
imp5 <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, maxit = 5, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
             print = FALSE)
imp10 <- mice.mids(imp5, maxit = 5, print = FALSE)
imp10$iteration

full <- mice(nhanes, m = 5, maxit = 10, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
             print = FALSE)
identical(complete(imp10, "long"), complete(full, "long"))
```

This works because the `mids` object stores how it was created
(`imp$future`), and the state of the random number stream of each chain
after the last iteration (`imp$chainSeed`).

You can also switch. `future = TRUE` continues a sequential object as
futures, for example to add many iterations to a model that you first
checked with a short sequential run. `future = FALSE` continues a
future object with the classic sampler, for example to see the
iteration history or to debug an imputation method:

```{r}
imp_seq <- mice.mids(imp5, maxit = 1, future = FALSE)
```

After a switch, the results are reproducible, but they differ from those
of a single call, because the random numbers come from other streams.

## Following the progress

For long runs, `mice()` can report its progress through the `progressr`
package. It signals one step after each iteration of each chain, so
`m * maxit` steps in total. With `future = TRUE`, the workers relay
these steps while the chains run. Nothing is shown unless you enable a
progress handler:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(progressr)
handlers("cli")

with_progress(
  imp <- mice(boys2, m = 20, maxit = 20, future = TRUE, print = FALSE)
)
```

To show the progress of every call in the session, use
`handlers(global = TRUE)` instead of `with_progress()`. The progress bar
disappears when the imputation has finished, so for a fast run you may
see nothing at all. Set `options(progressr.clear = FALSE)` to keep it.
Progress reporting does not change the imputations.

## User-written imputation methods

An imputation method is a function called `mice.impute.<name>()`. You
can write your own and use it in `method`. With `future = TRUE`,
`mice()` sends such functions to the workers, together with the objects
from your session that they use, such as helper functions:

```{r}
shrink <- function(x, f) mean(x) + f * (x - mean(x))

mice.impute.pmmshrink <- function(y, ry, x, ...) {
  shrink(mice.impute.pmm(y, ry, x, ...), f = 0.5)
}

meth <- make.method(nhanes)
meth["bmi"] <- "pmmshrink"
imp <- mice(nhanes, method = meth, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
            print = FALSE)
```

Imputation methods from other packages, such as those in `miceadds`,
are loaded on the workers automatically, but the package must be
installed on every worker.

## Post-processing per imputation

The argument `post` contains R code that is run after each imputation
of a variable. The code can use the variable `j`, the iteration `k`,
the column `i` of the imputations in `imp[[j]]`, and the imputation
number `chain`. A common use is to keep imputations within a range:

```{r}
post <- make.post(nhanes)
post["chl"] <- "imp[[j]][, i] <- squeeze(imp[[j]][, i], c(120, 300))"
```

Use `i` only to index `imp[[j]]`. With `future = TRUE`, each worker
holds a single chain, so `i` is always 1 there. For anything that should
differ between the imputations, use `chain`. For example, in a
sensitivity analysis that shifts the imputed values by an amount that
differs per imputation:

```{r}
delta <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20)
post["chl"] <- "imp[[j]][, i] <- imp[[j]][, i] + delta[chain]"
imp <- mice(nhanes, post = post, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
            print = FALSE)
```

With `future = FALSE`, `i` and `chain` are equal, so code that uses
`chain` works in both cases.

## When an imputation fails

If an imputation method or a `post` statement fails, `mice()` stops
with an error that tells where the sampler was. This works in the same
way with `future = TRUE`, where the failing chain stops all chains:

```{r, error = TRUE}
post <- make.post(nhanes)
post["bmi"] <- "if (k == 3 && chain == 4) stop('implausible values')"
imp <- mice(nhanes, post = post, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
            print = FALSE)
```

The error is a condition of class `mice_sampler_error`. Its fields
contain the details, and the field `parent` holds the original error:

```{r}
e <- tryCatch(
  mice(nhanes, post = post, seed = 1, future = TRUE,
       print = FALSE),
  error = identity
)
e[c("iteration", "imputation", "variable", "method", "post")]
e$parent
```

## Things to watch out for

* **The workers are separate R sessions.** They do not see the objects,
  packages and options of your session, except for what `mice()` sends
  them. Pass settings for an imputation method as arguments, for example
  through `...` or `blots`, rather than through `options()`.

* **Workers load the installed `mice`.** If you develop `mice` and load
  it with `devtools::load_all()`, the workers still use the version in
  your library. Install the package to test changes in parallel.

* **Workers run your startup files.** Each new worker reads
  `~/.Rprofile`. Code that is only meant for interactive use, such as
  loading development tools, slows down every worker and may produce
  warnings. Wrap such code in `if (interactive()) { ... }`.

* **Avoid parallelism within parallelism.** Some imputation methods use
  several threads themselves. Running such methods on many workers at
  once can oversubscribe the cores. `future` sets
  `parallelly::availableCores()` to 1 on its workers, and
  `method = "rf"` caps the threads of `ranger` and `literanger` at this
  value, so each chain uses one thread. This does not change the
  imputations. To use more threads per chain, set them yourself, e.g.
  `mice(..., method = "rf", num.threads = 2)` for `ranger` or
  `n_thread = 2` for `literanger`. Other methods, and a multithreaded
  BLAS library, are not limited automatically; use fewer workers for
  these.

* **Memory.** Each worker receives its own copy of the data and of the
  imputations of its chain. For large data, the memory use grows with
  the number of workers.

* **Number of cores.** `parallelly::availableCores()` respects the
  limits set by schedulers such as Slurm and by containers, and is a
  safer choice than `parallel::detectCores()`. Use `omit = 1` to keep a
  core free for the main process.

Close the workers when you are done:

```{r}
plan(sequential)
```
